prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Mathematical Notation Reference (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Symbol" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 2: header "Name" · longest unbreakable word 87px · one-line width 116px
  col 3: header "LaTeX" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 4: header "Meaning" · longest unbreakable word 111px · one-line width 1320px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 584px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 583px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 584px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Provide a reference linking mathematical symbols to their names, LaTeX commands, and meanings.","reading":"Readers can scan the symbol column to locate an entry, then read across for its name, command, and explanation; they may also compare names or commands down their columns.","groups":["Symbol, Name, and LaTeX identify the same notation in three forms.","Meaning explains each notation and contains the longest prose."],"keep_intact":["Symbols and LaTeX commands","Individual words in names and meanings","Column headers"],"may_wrap":["Meaning descriptions can wrap naturally at word boundaries.","Multiword names can wrap; their extra line may fit within the height already required by the meaning."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[82,137,87,277],"idea":"Keep names on one line and give the remaining space to the explanatory prose."},{"name":"B","widths":[82,108,87,306],"idea":"Use compact identifier columns and allow multiword names to wrap to give meanings the most room."},{"name":"C","widths":[105,126,105,247],"idea":"Give the three notation columns more breathing room for scanning while accepting more wrapping in meanings and longer names."}]}
